title: 22. Interview: Connection Pooling
summary: Interview Q&A for Connection Pooling — 14 questions with model answers.
objectives: Answer 14 Connection Pooling interview questions out loud
Lead with the concept, then a small example, then a tradeoff

sections.title: Conceptual Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. Why is opening a database connection so expensive?
**Answer:** A database connection is not just a TCP socket — it is a layered handshake. Steps: (1) TCP three-way handshake (1 RTT, ~1 ms LAN, ~100 ms cross-region). (2) Optional TLS negotiation (1–2 extra RTTs, plus asymmetric crypto on the client and server). (3) Authentication exchange — PostgreSQL's SCRAM-SHA-256 is 2–3 round-trips; MySQL's `caching_sha2_password` similar. (4) Server-side backend spawn — PostgreSQL forks a process (~5–10 MB RSS, ~1 ms on Linux); MySQL/SQL Server allocate a thread. (5) Session state setup — `SET search_path`, `SET timezone`, `SET statement_timeout`, etc. Each step adds latency; on a fast LAN the total is 5–15 ms, but across regions or with TLS+SCRAM it routinely exceeds 200 ms. If your query itself takes 2 ms, you have spent 96 % of the request on connection setup. The pool amortizes this setup across thousands of queries, dropping per-query overhead to ~0 ms. This is also why serverless platforms (Lambda) struggle with databases — cold starts recreate the connection every invocation, prompting tools like RDS Proxy and PlanetScale's Vitess proxy.
**Visual:**
```
Per-request connection cost (LAN, TLS, SCRAM):
  TCP SYN/ACK   ----->  1.0 ms   (1 RTT)
  TLS handshake ----->  2.0 ms   (2 RTTs)
  SCRAM auth    ----->  3.0 ms   (3 RTTs)
  SET params    ----->  1.0 ms
  Query exec    ----->  0.5 ms
  TOTAL: 7.5 ms (93 % overhead)

With pool: borrow(0) + query(0.5) + return(0) = 0.5 ms (0 % overhead)
```

### Q2. How do you choose the right pool size?
**Answer:** The classic formula from the PostgreSQL wiki and HikariCP is `pool_size ≈ (CPU_cores × 2) + effective_spindle_count`, generalized to `2 × cores + 1` on SSDs. The intuition: with N cores, N threads can be CPU-bound simultaneously; one or two more can be blocked on I/O without hurting throughput. Above that, connections thrash — context switches explode, CPU caches get evicted, and throughput drops even as concurrency rises. Real benchmarks: a 4-core PostgreSQL box peaks around 20 connections; doubling to 50 cuts throughput 30 %. The right approach is empirical: (1) Start with `2 × cores`. (2) Load-test sweeping sizes 5, 10, 20, 50, 100. (3) Find the throughput peak. (4) Back off 20 % for headroom. (5) Watch p99 latency, not just throughput — the peak throughput point often has rising tail latency, so size slightly below it. Also factor in: write-heavy workloads (longer transactions) tolerate fewer connections; read-only point queries tolerate more. And remember the server-side constraint — `max_connections` on PostgreSQL (default 100) must accommodate all pools across all app instances combined, which is where PgBouncer-style external pooling comes in.
**Visual:**
```
Throughput vs pool size (4-core box, SSD):
  QPS
   22k|                    *  <- peak (size=20)
   20k|              * *
   18k|         *
   15k|    *                   <- under-provisioned
   10k|
    5k|                            *  <- thrashing (size=100)
      +----+----+----+----+----+----> pool size
           5   10   20   50   100

Rule: peak ~ 2*cores+1; back off 20% for headroom
```

### Q3. What is LIFO vs FIFO eviction, and why does the choice matter?
**Answer:** LIFO (Last-In-First-Out) returns the most recently used connection — the "hot" one that just came back from a query. FIFO (First-In-First-Out) rotates through all connections evenly. LIFO is preferred for three reasons: (1) **Smaller working set** — a small subset of connections sees all traffic while the rest stay idle and get reaped by the idle timeout, freeing server-side memory. (2) **Cache warmth** — the connection's server-side backend keeps its buffer pool, plan cache, and relation cache hot, so repeated queries on the same connection skip re-planning. (3) **Lower steady-state backend count** — under low load, LIFO reaps idle connections aggressively; FIFO keeps them all open. The trade-off: LIFO can hide a "bad" connection (one whose backend is wedged but TCP is alive) because it keeps getting reused; FIFO would rotate past it. Modern pools (HikariCP) solve this with `ping_on_borrow` (`SELECT 1`) before handing out the connection, catching dead backends regardless of eviction order. PgBouncer defaults to LIFO; HikariCP is LIFO; the older Apache DBCP was FIFO and was notorious for stale-connection bugs.
**Visual:**
```
LIFO (HikariCP default):
  idle stack: [C5, C4, C3]  (C3 most recent)
  borrow -> C3 (hot, just used)
  return  -> C3 back on top
  -> C3,C4 always hot; C5 idle, reaped at 30s

FIFO (old DBCP):
  idle queue: [C3, C4, C5]
  borrow -> C3 (oldest)
  return  -> C3 back at end -> [C4, C5, C3]
  -> all 3 rotated; none reaped; more memory

LIFO wins on memory + cache warmth
FIFO wins on detecting dead conns (rotates past wedged backend)
```

### Q4. What is `max_lifetime` and why is it necessary?
**Answer:** `max_lifetime` is the maximum wall-clock time a connection can live before the pool forcibly closes and replaces it. Without it, connections live forever and accumulate drift: (1) **Plan cache drift** — a `ALTER TABLE` invalidates statistics, but the cached plan in the backend still uses old estimates; performance degrades mysteriously. (2) **Schema drift** — after a migration, the old connection may still see the old schema until it re-parses (rare but documented in MySQL). (3) **Memory leaks** — `work_mem` allocations, temp tables, and prepared statement caches accumulate across long sessions; a connection alive for a week can leak megabytes. (4) **Server-side config drift** — `SET statement_timeout` from one borrower leaks to the next if not reset; `max_lifetime` flushes these. (5) **Failover staleness** — after a failover, the old primary's connections are dead; `max_lifetime` recycles them naturally even if the pool doesn't notice. Typical values: 30 minutes (HikariCP, Netflix), 1 hour (PgBouncer `server_lifetime`). Too short wastes connections on churn (50 ms open cost repeated); too long lets drift accumulate and surface as confusing 3 AM performance bugs. The pool usually staggers closures (random jitter within 10 % of `max_lifetime`) to avoid closing all connections simultaneously.
**Visual:**
```
Connection lifetime drift:
  T=0min   open   ->  plan cache: empty, work_mem: 0
  T=5min   query  ->  plan cache: [Q1, Q2, Q3], work_mem: 2MB
  T=15min  query  ->  plan cache: [Q1..Q10], work_mem: 8MB (leak!)
  T=20min  ALTER TABLE happens (other conn)
  T=25min  query  ->  uses STALE plan from T=5min, slow
  T=30min  max_lifetime -> CLOSE, open new conn (clean state)

Without max_lifetime: drift accumulates forever
With max_lifetime=30min: drift bounded to 30 min
```

### Q5. What is the difference between session-mode and transaction-mode pooling (PgBouncer)?
**Answer:** PgBouncer (and similar external poolers) operates in two main modes. **Session mode** assigns a server connection to a client for the lifetime of the client's session — PgBouncer only reclaims the connection when the client disconnects. This is the safest mode (prepared statements, SET variables, advisory locks, temporary tables all work) but provides the least pooling benefit — if 1000 clients connect, you need 1000 server connections, which defeats the purpose. **Transaction mode** assigns a server connection only for the duration of a transaction — when the client sends `COMMIT` or `ROLLBACK`, the connection returns to the pool and can be reused by a different client. This provides massive multiplexing (1000 clients on 50 server connections) but breaks anything that relies on session state: prepared statements (`PREPARE` then `EXECUTE` across transactions), `SET` variables (reset between transactions), advisory locks, `LISTEN/NOTIFY`, and temporary tables. Netflix's PgBouncer in front of RDS uses transaction mode for billing — they rewrote the app to avoid session-state features (use query parameters instead of PREPARE, set variables per-transaction). The trade-off: transaction mode is 10–100× more efficient but requires application discipline. Session mode works with any app but provides little benefit. A third mode, **statement mode**, releases the connection after every statement — even more efficient but breaks multi-statement transactions entirely; rarely used.
**Visual:**
```
PgBouncer modes (1000 clients, max 50 server conns):

Session mode:
  client1 ---conn1---> server1   (held entire session)
  client2 ---conn2---> server2
  ...1000 clients...  -> ERROR: max_connections exceeded
  Pooling benefit: NONE (1:1 client:server)

Transaction mode:
  client1 BEGIN; Q1; COMMIT  -- uses server1 for ~5ms, returns
  client2 BEGIN; Q2; COMMIT  -- uses server1 next (multiplexed!)
  ...1000 clients multiplexed onto 50 servers...
  Pooling benefit: 20x reduction in server backends

  Limitations: no PREPARE/EXECUTE across txn, no SET, no LISTEN
```

### Q6. How does a pool detect and handle a dead connection?
**Answer:** Connections die silently — the server kills the backend (OOM, restart), the network drops (NAT timeout, firewall idle reaper), or a failover rewrites the IP. The TCP socket may stay half-open for hours, so the pool can't rely on the OS to tell it. Detection strategies: (1) **Ping on borrow** — run `SELECT 1` (or a no-op like `/* ping */ SELECT 1`) before handing the connection to the caller. Catches dead connections at borrow time. Cost: 1 extra round-trip per borrow (~0.5 ms LAN). HikariCP uses this with `connectionTestQuery`. (2) **Ping on return** — validate when the connection comes back, before pushing to idle. Less common. (3) **Keepalive** — TCP keepalive (`SO_KEEPALIVE`) probes idle sockets; default Linux is 2 hours, tunable to 30 seconds. Doesn't catch all death modes but free. (4) **Driver-level isValid** — JDBC's `Connection.isValid(timeout)` uses the driver's native protocol-level ping (PostgreSQL's `Parse/Bind/Execute` of `SELECT 1`, MySQL's `COM_PING`) — cheaper than running a query. (5) **Reaper thread** — background thread periodically pings idle connections and closes dead ones. When a dead connection is detected, the pool closes it, decrements `in_use`, and the next borrower either gets a fresh connection (if under `max_size`) or waits. The caller never sees the dead connection. Real-world: HikariCP combines `isValid` on borrow with a 30-second housekeeper thread that closes dead idle connections.
**Visual:**
```
Connection death detection:
  +---------+      +---------+
  | Pool    |--->  | Server  | (backend OOM-killed at T=10s)
  +---------+      +---------+
       |              |
       |  (TCP still ESTABLISHED -- no FIN/RST!)
       |
  T=11s: borrower requests conn
  borrow(): ping (SELECT 1) -> TIMEOUT after 1s
  -> close dead conn, decrement in_use
  -> open fresh conn (or wait if at max)
  -> caller never sees the dead conn

  Without ping_on_borrow: caller gets dead conn,
                          first query fails -> user-facing error
```

### Q7. What happens when the pool is exhausted and a borrower times out?
**Answer:** When `in_use == max_size` and the idle stack is empty, a borrower waits on a bounded queue for `borrow_timeout` seconds (typically 1–5 s). If a connection is returned before the timeout, the borrower takes it and proceeds. If not, the borrower gets a `PoolTimeoutException` (HikariCP) or `TimeoutError` (Python pools) — the application must handle this as a transient error and either retry with backoff or return a 503 to the user. Critical design choices: (1) **Always have a timeout** — an unbounded `borrow()` lets request threads pile up indefinitely, cascading into thread-pool exhaustion and full outage. (2) **Fail fast, not slow** — a 1-second timeout that returns 503 is better than a 30-second hang that fills up the app server's thread pool and triggers a GC storm. (3) **Circuit break above the pool** — if the pool is chronically exhausted, the database is the bottleneck; a circuit breaker (Hystrix, Resilience4j) should shed load until the database recovers. (4) **Monitor pool wait time** — p99 wait > 50 ms means the pool is undersized or the database is slow; alert on it. (5) **Never block the caller's thread synchronously if you can avoid it** — async drivers (pgx for Go, asyncpg for Python, R2DBC for Java) compose with async frameworks and avoid thread exhaustion. Real-world: Netflix's Hystrix circuit-breaker trips when pool wait exceeds 5 seconds, returning a fallback response and preventing cascading failure.
**Visual:**
```
Pool exhaustion timeline:
  T=0    borrow() -> pool empty, in_use=20 (max)
  T=0    wait on queue (timeout=2s)
  T=0.5  another thread returns conn -> borrower takes it
  T=0.5  SUCCESS

  vs. chronic overload:
  T=0    borrow() -> pool empty
  T=2s   PoolTimeoutException
  T=2s   app returns 503 (or retries with backoff)
  T=2s   circuit breaker increments failure count
  T=10s  breaker trips -> fast-fail all requests
  T=30s  breaker half-open -> probe
  T=32s  probe succeeds -> close breaker, resume traffic

  No timeout -> threads pile up -> app server hangs -> outage
```

sections.title: Scenario-Based Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. Netflix's billing service runs 4000 microservice instances, each with a pool of 5 against a single RDS PostgreSQL `max_connections=1600`. Connection errors spike during peak. How do you fix it?
**Answer:** Classic over-subscription: 4000 instances × 5 connections = 20,000 potential server connections, but RDS caps at 1600. During peak, pools open more connections, RDS rejects new ones with `FATAL: too many connections`, and apps fail. The fix is **external pooling with PgBouncer in front of RDS**: deploy PgBouncer (or RDS Proxy) as a sidecar or shared service; app pools now connect to PgBouncer (cheap, local), and PgBouncer multiplexes them onto a small fixed set of server connections (say 50–100). With PgBouncer in transaction mode, 20,000 client connections share 50 server backends — a 400× reduction. Per-backend memory drops from 200 GB (20k × 10 MB) to 500 MB. p99 query latency drops because PostgreSQL stops context-switching. Trade-offs: (1) Transaction mode breaks PREPARE/EXECUTE and session SET — refactor the app to use query parameters and per-transaction settings. (2) PgBouncer itself needs HA — deploy 2–3 instances behind a load balancer. (3) Latency adds ~0.5 ms per query for the PgBouncer hop. (4) Long-running transactions (>1 s) hold server connections and break multiplexing — set `statement_timeout` and `idle_in_transaction_timeout`. Real-world: Netflix uses exactly this pattern — PgBouncer sidecars in front of RDS, transaction mode, billing service handles 50k QPS on a `db.r5.12xlarge` without connection errors.
**Visual:**
```
Before: 4000 instances x pool=5 = 20,000 -> RDS max=1600 -> FAIL
  App1(5) --+
  App2(5) --+--> RDS (max=1600) -> "too many connections"
  ...4000...+

After: PgBouncer sidecar per instance, transaction mode
  App1(pool=5) --> PgBouncer1 ---+
  App2(pool=5) --> PgBouncer2 ---+--> RDS (max=1600, using only ~50)
  ...4000...                     +
                                50 server backends multiplexing 20k clients
  Memory: 200GB -> 500MB
  p99 latency: 80ms -> 8ms (no ctx switching)
```

### Q2. Your application's p99 latency spikes to 500 ms every few hours for 30 seconds, then recovers. Pool size is 20, max_connections is 100. How do you diagnose?
**Answer:** Intermittent latency spikes suggest pool starvation during bursts — callers wait for a connection, then succeed when one frees up. Diagnosis: (1) **Check pool wait time** — instrument `borrow()` to record wait duration; if p99 wait spikes to 500 ms during the spike, the pool is the bottleneck. (2) **Check query latency** — if `borrow()` is instant but `query()` is slow, the database is the bottleneck (slow query, lock contention, vacuum). (3) **Check in_use count** — if `in_use == max_size` during the spike, the pool is exhausted. (4) **Check for long-running transactions** — `SELECT * FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE state='active' AND now()-query_start > interval '5 seconds'`; a single 30-second query holds a connection and starves others. (5) **Check for connection leaks** — if `in_use` monotonically rises and never drops, a code path forgot to `return_conn()` (exception swallowed before `finally`). (6) **Check traffic pattern** — is there a cron job, batch process, or retry storm hitting the pool every few hours? Likely causes: a slow analytical query hogging a connection; a leaked connection slowly exhausting the pool; a retry storm from a downstream service amplifying load. Fixes: add `statement_timeout=5s` to kill runaway queries; use try/finally to guarantee `return_conn()`; isolate analytical queries to a separate pool; add a circuit breaker to shed load during spikes. Real-world: Netflix's billing service had a leak where a `except:` block swallowed the `return_conn()` call; pool drained over 6 hours then collapsed — fixed with try/finally and a leak detector that logs when a connection is held > 1 s.
**Visual:**
```
Diagnosis tree:
  p99 500ms spike
     |
     +-- borrow() wait spike?  -> YES: pool exhausted
     |       +-- in_use==max?  -> YES: too few conns or leak
     |       |     +-- rises monotonically? -> LEAK (missing finally)
     |       |     +-- burst of traffic?    -> undersized pool
     |       +-- in_use<max? -> POOL_TIMEOUT (network?)
     |
     +-- borrow() fast, query() slow? -> DB bottleneck
             +-- pg_stat_activity shows long query? -> slow query
             +-- lock contention?        -> pg_locks
             +-- vacuum running?         -> pg_stat_progress_vacuum

Fixes: try/finally return_conn, statement_timeout, separate analytics pool,
       circuit breaker for downstream retries, monitor borrow_wait p99
```

### Q3. You migrate from a single PostgreSQL instance to a primary + 3 read replicas. After migration, p99 read latency triples. What went wrong?
**Answer:** The most common cause: the application's pool still points at the primary, and the "read replicas" aren't actually being used. Or: the pool now routes reads to replicas but the replicas are lagging, so reads block waiting for replication. Diagnosis: (1) **Verify routing** — check `pg_stat_activity` on primary vs replicas; if the primary still sees all the read load, the app's router isn't configured. (2) **Check replica lag** — `SELECT * FROM pg_stat_replication` on the primary; if lag is seconds, the replica is overloaded. (3) **Check pool count** — if the app opened a pool per replica (3 × pool=20 = 60 connections total), but each replica only handles 1/3 the load, you have over-provisioned pools and cache-thrashing on each replica. (4) **Check connection string** — many ORM routers require explicit `read_endpoints` config; missing it routes all reads to the primary. (5) **Check for cross-region latency** — if replicas are in another region for disaster recovery, reads routed to them incur 50–100 ms cross-region latency. (6) **Check the replica's hardware** — replicas often get smaller instances than the primary; the replica is CPU-bound. Fixes: configure read/write split in the ORM; size replicas to match primary; keep read replicas in-region for low-latency reads; use cross-region replicas only for DR. Real-world: a common migration mistake is forgetting to update `DATABASE_READ_REPLICA_URL` env var, so the app keeps reading from the primary; the replicas sit idle while the primary is overloaded.
**Visual:**
```
Migration: 1 primary -> 1 primary + 3 replicas, p99 triples

  Before:  all reads+writes -> Primary (pool=20)
           Primary CPU 60%, p99=10ms

  After:   writes -> Primary, reads -> ??
           Primary CPU 90% (still all reads!), replicas idle, p99=30ms
                              ^ BUG: router not configured

  Fix:     DATABASE_READ_REPLICA_URL=replica1,replica2,replica3
           ORM router: readOnly=true -> replica pool

  Common gotchas:
    + router not configured -> reads still hit primary
    + cross-region replica for reads -> 100ms penalty
    + replica sized smaller than primary -> CPU-bound
    + replica lag >1s -> reads block on stale data
```

### Q4. You're building a serverless API on AWS Lambda hitting PostgreSQL. Cold starts take 2 seconds; warm invocations are 10 ms. How do you optimize?
**Answer:** Lambda cold starts pay the full connection cost — TCP, TLS, SCRAM auth — every time a new container spins up, which can be every few minutes under spiky traffic. Fixes in priority order: (1) **Use RDS Proxy** — AWS-managed PgBouncer-like pooler that maintains a warm pool of connections to RDS; Lambda connects to the proxy (fast local connect), and the proxy multiplexes onto a small set of RDS backends. Cold-start connection cost drops from 2 s to ~50 ms. (2) **Reuse the connection across invocations** — Lambda's execution context is reused between invocations on the same container; initialize the pool outside the handler (`pool = ConnectionPool(...)` at module level) so warm invocations skip pool initialization entirely. (3) **Provisioned concurrency** — keep N Lambda containers warm to eliminate cold starts entirely; trade-off: cost (you pay for N containers 24/7). (4) **Use IAM auth instead of password** — AWS RDS IAM auth uses short-lived tokens, avoiding SCRAM overhead, but adds STS call latency; net win only for very high connection churn. (5) **Reduce TLS overhead** — use RDS Proxy's TLS termination so Lambda connects over plain TCP locally. (6) **Avoid prepared statements** — they break PgBouncer's transaction mode. Real-world: AWS's own guidance for Lambda+RDS is "always use RDS Proxy" — it solves both the cold-start connection cost and the `max_connections` exhaustion that 1000 concurrent Lambdas would otherwise cause. Netflix's serverless video encoding triggers use exactly this pattern.
**Visual:**
```
Lambda + RDS, before optimization:
  Cold start: container init(500ms) + DB conn(2000ms) + query(10ms) = 2.5s
  Warm:       DB conn cached(0ms) + query(10ms) = 10ms
  Problem: spiky traffic -> many cold starts -> 2.5s p99

With RDS Proxy:
  Cold start: container init(500ms) + proxy connect(50ms) + query(10ms) = 560ms
  Warm:       10ms (same)
  Proxy multiplexes 1000 Lambdas onto ~20 RDS backends

With provisioned concurrency (N=10):
  Cold start: NEVER (containers always warm)
  Warm:       10ms
  Cost:       10 containers x 24h = expensive but no cold starts

Layered fix: RDS Proxy + module-level pool + provisioned concurrency
```

### Q5. A junior engineer sets the pool `max_size=500` "to be safe." The database is now slower than when `max_size=20`. Explain why.
**Answer:** This is the most common pool-sizing mistake. More connections do not mean more throughput — they mean more contention. PostgreSQL (and MySQL, SQL Server) share CPU, memory, and disk across all backends. With 500 connections on a 4-core box: (1) **Context-switching dominates** — the OS scheduler thrashes between 500 threads, each getting a tiny time slice; CPU cycles that should run your query are spent switching. (2) **Cache thrashing** — each backend has its own buffer pool, plan cache, and relation cache; with 500 backends, the CPU L1/L2/L3 caches evict each other constantly. (3) **Lock contention** — 500 backends compete for the same row locks, page locks, and WAL lock; the wait queue grows. (4) **Memory pressure** — 500 × 10 MB = 5 GB just for idle backends; if the box has 8 GB, the database is now swapping. (5) **WAL contention** — 500 backends writing to the same WAL is serialized; throughput caps at WAL bandwidth regardless of connection count. Benchmarks consistently show throughput peaking at ~`2 × cores + spindles` then declining; at 500 connections on a 4-core box, throughput is often 1/4 of the peak. The fix: cap the pool at `2 × cores + 1` (use PgBouncer for multiplexing if more app concurrency is needed), and use a queue + circuit breaker to shed excess load. Real-world: HikariCP's documentation explicitly warns against this; the formula `2 × cores + 1` comes from a 2012 PostgreSQL benchmark that's been validated dozens of times since.
**Visual:**
```
Throughput vs pool size (4-core, 8GB RAM, SSD):

  QPS
  22k|              *  <- peak (size=22, ~2*cores)
  18k|         *
  12k|    *                *  <- junior's "safe" size=500
   5k|                            *
      +----+----+----+----+----+----> pool size
           5   20   50  100  500

  Why 500 is worse:
    + context switches: 500 threads on 4 cores = 125x oversubscription
    + L3 cache evicted across 500 backends
    + WAL lock contention (serialized writes)
    + 5GB RAM on idle backends -> swap
    + Lock wait queues grow -> p99 explodes

  Fix: pool=20 + PgBouncer for multiplexing + queue + circuit breaker
```

### Q6. You're seeing intermittent `Connection reset by peer` errors in production. The pool is configured correctly. What else could cause it?
**Answer:** "Pool is configured correctly" means the pool itself isn't the problem — but the network, the database, or the OS between them is. Causes: (1) **NAT/firewall idle reaping** — AWS NLB has a 350-second idle timeout; if a connection sits idle in the pool longer than that, the NLB silently drops it; the next borrow gets a dead socket. Fix: set `idle_timeout < NAT_timeout` (e.g., 300 s) or enable TCP keepalive. (2) **Database restart** — RDS maintenance window, failover, parameter-group change; all server connections die. Pool should detect via `ping_on_borrow` and reconnect. (3) **OOM killer** — the server runs out of memory and the OOM killer reaps PostgreSQL backends; the client sees RST. Fix: tune `work_mem`, add RAM, or set `oom_score_adj`. (4) **Network blips** — cross-AZ or cross-region connections drop on transient network issues; fix with retry logic. (5) **`tcp_keepalive` too lax** — default Linux keepalive is 2 hours; the connection can be dead for 2 hours before the OS notices. Set `tcp_keepalive_time=30s`, `tcp_keepalive_intvl=10s`, `tcp_keepalive_probes=3`. (6) **Connection limit hit** — if the pool opens connections aggressively, it can hit `max_connections` on the DB; the DB sends RST. (7) **Driver bug** — older JDBC/psycopg2 versions had bugs that caused silent socket death; upgrade. Diagnosis: enable pool logging (HikariCP has `housekeeping-period` logs), check `pg_stat_activity` for backend counts, check `dmesg` for OOM kills, check NLB access logs for idle reaping. Real-world: Netflix had a week-long hunt for connection resets that turned out to be the AWS NLB 350 s idle timeout — fixed by setting `idle_timeout=300s` on HikariCP.
**Visual:**
```
Connection reset by peer - root cause tree:

  Pool OK?
   +-- idle > NAT/firewall timeout?  -> AWS NLB 350s, fix idle_timeout
   +-- DB restarted?                 -> failover/maintenance, ping_on_borrow
   +-- OOM kill?                     -> dmesg, tune work_mem, add RAM
   +-- tcp_keepalive lax?            -> default 2h, set to 30s/10s/3
   +-- max_connections hit?          -> check pg_stat_activity count
   +-- network blip (cross-AZ)?      -> retry with backoff
   +-- driver bug?                   -> upgrade JDBC/psycopg2

  Diagnosis: enable pool logging, watch pg_stat_activity, dmesg,
             NLB logs, check tcp_keepalive_time on the client
```

### Q7. You're using HikariCP. The application crashes on startup with `PoolInitializationException: Failed to get connection within 30 seconds`. How do you debug?
**Answer:** HikariCP opens `min_size` connections at startup; if any fail within `initializationTimeout` (default 30 s), the pool refuses to start (fail-fast — better than running with a half-dead pool). Debug steps: (1) **Verify connectivity from the app host** — `psql -h <host> -U <user> <db>` or `telnet <host> 5432`; if this fails, it's a network/security-group issue. (2) **Check security groups / firewall** — does the app's security group allow outbound to the DB's port? Does the DB's security group allow inbound from the app? Common mistake: SG allows the app's old subnet but not the new one after a deploy. (3) **Check credentials** — wrong password, wrong username, wrong database name; check the JDBC URL. (4) **Check `max_connections`** — if the pool can't open `min_size` connections because `max_connections` is exhausted, all `min_size` opens fail. (5) **Check DNS resolution** — `nslookup <db-host>`; RDS endpoints are DNS names; if DNS is slow or fails, the connection fails. (6) **Check TLS** — if the DB requires TLS and the JDBC URL doesn't have `?sslmode=require`, the connection is rejected. (7) **Check HikariCP config** — `initializationFailTimeout` > 0 means fail-fast; set to 0 to start lazily (not recommended for production). (8) **Check the DB itself** — `SELECT 1` from another client; is the DB up? Is it in recovery? Real-world: 80 % of `PoolInitializationException` cases are security-group misconfigurations after a deployment; 15 % are wrong credentials; 5 % are actual DB outages. Always check network first.

  4. Check HikariCP config:
     - jdbcUrl correct? (host, port, db, sslmode)
     - username/password match?
     - initializationFailTimeout > 0 (fail-fast)?
